title: Suspend on MacBookPro14,2: keep Wi-Fi and USB-C working across S3 (two systemd-sleep hooks)
author: bjhinkle
body:
## Summary

This adds two `systemd-sleep` hooks and a short "Suspend" section for the recipe. With them, a 2017 13-inch MacBook Pro (MacBookPro14,2, Apple T1) suspends to S3 and comes back with Wi-Fi and USB-C working, which it does not do with the stock setup. Everything below was measured on one machine over about twenty suspend cycles on 2026-09-05.

Environment: Omarchy 4.0.2, kernel 7.1.9-arch1-2, Mac firmware 529.140.2.0.0, this repository at 8e479f0 (unmodified), `snd_hda_macbookpro` at ef27884.

## Problem 1: Wi-Fi dies on about half of resumes

On resume the BCM43602 sometimes keeps its PCI registers readable while its firmware is dead. `brcmfmac` then takes its hot-resume path, trusts the dead firmware, and every command times out. Wi-Fi is gone until the driver is reloaded or the machine rebooted. Which path it takes is a coin flip.

Fix: `brcmfmac-reload` unloads `brcmfmac_wcc` and `brcmfmac` before sleep and reloads them after, so every resume takes the full re-probe path. Measured on more than a dozen S3 cycles: interface present within a second of resume, associated within about ten seconds, same IP. The NVRAM calibration file is re-read on each reload, so nothing else changes.

## Problem 2: Thunderbolt and USB-C are dead after every suspend

The platform firmware removes power from the Alpine Ridge controllers in S3 regardless of what the kernel asks. On resume the bridges come back with collapsed windows, the kernel cannot re-allocate them at runtime ("can't assign; no space"), pciehp removes both Thunderbolt-side xHCI controllers, and USB-C is gone until a power cycle. The Touch Bar, keyboard, audio and camera survive because the T1 sits on the chipset's own xHCI.

Things that do not help, all measured: `d3cold_allowed=0` on every device in the tree (the ports failed from D3hot, not D3cold), `pcie_port_pm=off`, `pcie_ports=compat`, forcing the root ports to D0 and rescanning, and evaluating the firmware's own power-on methods with `acpi_call` (the GPIO pads read the same on a dead side and a live side; the rails belong to the platform).

What does help: remove the two Thunderbolt upstream ports (`03:00.0` and `79:00.0`, the children of root ports `00:1c.4` and `00:1d.0`) cleanly before sleep, and rescan after resume. The chipset root ports never lose their windows, so the rescan re-enumerates the whole tree with fresh assignment. `thunderbolt-remove-rescan` does that, plus:

- it runs `sync` first and skips a side if a mounted filesystem is reached through it (a USB-C disk would otherwise be torn before the kernel's suspend sync);
- it disables S3 wake on the four PCIe root ports (they share one wake line, and nothing on them needs to wake a laptop; runtime hot-plug is unaffected);
- it waits for the two root ports to runtime-suspend (typically 2 ms, capped at 5 s);
- after resume it rescans once and, if the tree is not back within 2 s, hands retries to a transient unit with `systemd-run --collect`, because post hooks run while `user.slice` is still frozen and a plain backgrounded subshell is killed with the hook;
- every path exits 0, so it can never block a suspend.

Measured behaviour with the hook installed:

- Sleeps of about 80 s or more: the full tree is back on the first rescan (32 PCI functions, six USB root hubs, three xHCI controllers, links at 8 GT/s). A tree that was live at sleep entry came back after 47 s.
- Sleeps of about 7 s or less: the tree is dead afterwards, and comes back on the next sleep of a few minutes (one side after about 80 s, both after about six minutes; 362 s is the shortest measured for both). A reboot is never needed. USB-C still works at USB 2.0 through the chipset controller in the meantime, so a short sleep costs SuperSpeed and Thunderbolt, not the ports.
- The tree comes back on new bus numbers below the upstream ports (the two xHCI controllers moved from `06:00.0` and `7c:00.0` to `2c:00.0` and `a2:00.0`, the same numbers on every cycle). Nothing may key on addresses below `03:00.0` or `79:00.0`.

Not covered: hibernate (the hook acts on plain suspend only), external displays over USB-C across a sleep, and Thunderbolt PCIe devices.

## One thing to expect

Lid-closed sleeps sometimes wake on their own about 6 to 8 s in and then re-suspend a few seconds later; that short sleep leaves the tree dead as above until the next long sleep. Every wake source the kernel can see was ruled out with controls (GPE counters, wakeup sources, the PM1 status register, the raw GPE0 block); the cause is firmware-side. `in ordinary use so far: one of three lid-closes`.

One more scope note: this is for the keyboard-mode Touch Bar stack (apple-ib-tb lineage). The t1bridge display-mode stack replaces those drivers and lists sleep/wake as not working; these hooks may still apply there since they touch Thunderbolt and Wi-Fi, not the T1, but that is untested.

## Files

- `default/systemd/system-sleep/brcmfmac-reload` and `default/systemd/system-sleep/thunderbolt-remove-rescan`: the two hooks, beside the packaged `keyboard-backlight`, `force-igpu` and `unmount-fuse`. Root-owned 0755, every path exits 0, `thunderbolt-remove-rescan` acts on plain suspend only.
- `install/hardware/apple/fix-t1-suspend.sh`: installs both when `product_name` matches `MacBookPro13,[123]` or `MacBookPro14,[123]`, wired into `install/hardware/all.sh` after `fix-brcmfmac-supplicant.sh`.
- `migrations/1789242220.sh`: the same for existing installs; leaves a hook alone if the user already carries an identical copy. Nothing to restart; the hooks take effect at the next suspend.

The Thunderbolt hook finds the upstream ports from the NHIs bound to the `thunderbolt` driver (NHI, downstream port, upstream port), so no PCI addresses are hard-coded; it disables S3 wake on the PCIe root ports (they share one wake line, and nothing on them needs to wake a laptop; runtime hot-plug keys on the wake capability, not this flag). Delete the two files to undo.

## How this was tested

Hands-off cycles with an RTC alarm as the only wake (`echo $(( $(date +%s) + 100 )) > /sys/class/rtc/rtc0/wakealarm; systemctl suspend`), with the tree counted before and after by `ls /sys/bus/pci/devices | wc -l`, `ls -d /sys/bus/usb/devices/usb*`, and `ls /sys/bus/pci/drivers/xhci_hcd`, and the journal grepped for `can't assign`, `Unable to change power state` and `Host halt failed`. Then five real lid-close cycles, then daily use. Anyone reproducing this should touch nothing for the first ten seconds of a lid-open sleep; an early wake strands the tree.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

@@ -0,0 +1,59 @@
+#!/bin/bash
+# Reload the Broadcom brcmfmac Wi-Fi driver around every sleep on Macs.
+#
+# On resume from S3 the BCM43602 in the 2016-2017 MacBook Pros sometimes keeps
+# its PCI registers readable while its firmware is dead. brcmfmac then takes its
+# hot-resume path, trusts the dead firmware, every command times out, and only
+# a driver reload or a reboot brings Wi-Fi back. Which path it takes is a coin
+# flip. Unloading the driver before sleep forces the full re-probe with a
+# firmware reload after resume, the path that always works. Measured on a
+# MacBookPro14,2 over more than thirty suspend cycles: interface present within
+# a second of resume, associated within about ten seconds, same address.
+#
+# Never blocks sleep: every path exits 0. Logs to the journal as
+# brcmfmac-reload. Delete this file to undo.
+
+MODS="brcmfmac_wcc brcmfmac"      # unload order matters: brcmfmac_wcc uses brcmfmac
+STATE=/run/brcmfmac-reload.state
+
+log() { logger -t brcmfmac-reload -- "$*"; }
+loaded() { grep -q '^brcmfmac ' /proc/modules; }
+# Any network interface whose PCI device is bound to brcmfmac.
+iface() { ls -d /sys/bus/pci/drivers/brcmfmac/0000:*/net/* 2>/dev/null | head -1 | xargs -r basename; }
+
+case "$1" in
+  pre)
+    rm -f "$STATE"
+    if ! loaded; then
+      echo absent >"$STATE"; log "pre/$2: brcmfmac not loaded, nothing to do"
+    elif timeout 60 modprobe -r $MODS; then
+      echo unloaded >"$STATE"; log "pre/$2: unloaded $MODS"
+    else
+      echo failed >"$STATE"; log "pre/$2: WARNING unload failed, driver left loaded"
+    fi
+    ;;
+  post)
+    state=$(cat "$STATE" 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
+    if [[ $state != unloaded ]] && loaded; then
+      # pre could not unload (or its state was lost): force the reload now
+      if timeout 60 modprobe -r $MODS; then
+        log "post/$2: late unload ok (pre state: $state)"
+      else
+        log "post/$2: WARNING late unload failed (pre state: $state); leaving driver as is"
+        rm -f "$STATE"; exit 0
+      fi
+    fi
+    if modprobe brcmfmac; then
+      for ((i = 0; i < 40; i++)); do [[ -n $(iface) ]] && break; sleep 0.5; done
+      if [[ -n $(iface) ]]; then
+        log "post/$2: reloaded, $(iface) present after $((i / 2))s"
+      else
+        log "post/$2: WARNING reloaded but no brcmfmac interface after 20s"
+      fi
+    else
+      log "post/$2: ERROR modprobe brcmfmac failed"
+    fi
+    rm -f "$STATE"
+    ;;
+esac
+exit 0

@@ -0,0 +1,155 @@
+#!/bin/bash
+# Keep Thunderbolt and USB-C working across S3 on the 2016-2017 MacBook Pros
+# (MacBookPro13,x and 14,x, Intel Alpine Ridge).
+#
+# The platform firmware removes power from the Thunderbolt controllers in S3
+# whatever the kernel asks. After that dirty loss the switch bridges come back
+# with collapsed windows, the kernel cannot re-assign them at runtime ("bridge
+# window ... can't assign; no space"), pciehp removes the Thunderbolt-side xHCI
+# controllers, and USB-C is dead until a power cycle. Kernel-side levers
+# (d3cold_allowed, pcie_port_pm=off, pcie_ports=compat) do not help; the rails
+# are the platform's.
+#
+# What works: remove the Thunderbolt upstream ports cleanly before sleep, so the
+# chipset root ports keep their windows, and rescan after resume, so the tree
+# is re-enumerated with fresh assignment. Measured on a MacBookPro14,2 over
+# about thirty suspend cycles: a sleep of a minute or more brings the whole
+# tree back on the first rescan; a sleep of a few seconds hands back a
+# controller that never finished powering down, and the tree stays dead until
+# the next sleep of a few minutes (USB 2.0 keeps working meanwhile through the
+# chipset's own xHCI). The tree returns on new bus numbers below the upstream
+# ports, so nothing may key on addresses below them.
+#
+# Design:
+# - Upstream ports are found from the NHIs bound to the thunderbolt driver
+#   (NHI -> downstream port -> upstream port), never from fixed addresses.
+# - pre: sync first; a side with a mounted filesystem reached through its
+#   upstream port is NOT removed (it would be torn before the kernel's suspend
+#   sync) and gets the dead-until-later outcome instead of data loss.
+# - pre: S3 wake is disabled on the PCIe root ports (they share one wake line;
+#   nothing on them needs to wake a laptop). Not restored: the sysfs flag only
+#   governs system sleep, runtime hot-plug keys on the wake capability, and a
+#   reboot resets it.
+# - pre: wait until the Thunderbolt root ports report runtime_status=suspended
+#   (milliseconds in practice; capped at 5 s).
+# - post: one rescan; if the tree is not back within 2 s, retries go to a
+#   transient unit via systemd-run, because post hooks run while user.slice is
+#   frozen and a backgrounded subshell dies with the hook
+#   (systemd-suspend.service is Type=oneshot with KillMode=control-group).
+# - Acts on plain suspend only. Every path exits 0, so it can never block
+#   sleep. Journal tag: thunderbolt-remove-rescan. Delete this file to undo.
+
+STATE=/run/thunderbolt-remove-rescan.roots
+log()  { logger -t thunderbolt-remove-rescan -- "$*"; }
+xhci() { ls /sys/bus/pci/drivers/xhci_hcd 2>/dev/null | grep -c '^0000'; }
+
+# Print "<upstream port sysfs path> <root port sysfs path>" for every
+# Thunderbolt controller whose NHI is currently bound.
+thunderbolt_ports() {
+  local nhi d up
+  for nhi in /sys/bus/pci/drivers/thunderbolt/0000:*; do
+    [[ -e $nhi ]] || continue
+    d=$(readlink -f "$nhi") || continue
+    up=$(dirname "$(dirname "$d")")
+    [[ -e $up/remove ]] || continue
+    printf '%s %s\n' "$up" "$(dirname "$up")"
+  done | sort -u
+}
+roots_from_state() { [[ -f $STATE ]] && awk '{print $2}' "$STATE" | sort -u; }
+links() {
+  local rp s
+  for rp in $(roots_from_state); do
+    s=$(cat "$rp/current_link_speed" 2>/dev/null); printf '%s=%s ' "$(basename "$rp")" "${s:-?}"
+  done
+}
+state() { echo "xhci=$(xhci) pci=$(ls /sys/bus/pci/devices | wc -l) links: $(links)"; }
+
+# Is block device $1 (a name under /sys/class/block) reached through PCI device
+# $2 (a sysfs path)? Follows dm/md slaves, so LUKS or RAID on a USB-C disk counts.
+under_port() {
+  local p s
+  p=$(readlink -f "/sys/class/block/$1" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
+  [[ $p == "$2"/* ]] && return 0
+  for s in "/sys/class/block/$1"/slaves/*; do
+    [[ -e $s ]] && under_port "${s##*/}" "$2" && return 0
+  done
+  return 1
+}
+# Print the first mounted device reached through PCI device $1, if any.
+mounted_under() {
+  local dev b
+  while read -r dev _; do
+    [[ $dev == /dev/* ]] || continue
+    b=$(readlink -f "$dev" 2>/dev/null) || continue
+    under_port "${b##*/}" "$1" && { echo "$dev"; return 0; }
+  done < /proc/mounts
+  return 1
+}
+
+if [[ $2 != suspend && $1 != retry ]]; then
+  exit 0
+fi
+
+case "$1" in
+  pre)
+    sync
+    thunderbolt_ports >"$STATE"
+    n=0; skipped=0
+    while read -r up rp; do
+      [[ -n $up ]] || continue
+      if m=$(mounted_under "$up"); then
+        log "pre/$2: WARNING $m is mounted through $(basename "$up") - NOT removing it (USB-C on that side stays down until a later sleep; no torn filesystem)"
+        skipped=$((skipped + 1)); continue
+      fi
+      if echo 1 > "$up/remove" 2>/dev/null; then
+        n=$((n + 1)); log "pre/$2: removed $(basename "$up") (under $(basename "$rp"))"
+      else
+        log "pre/$2: WARNING could not remove $(basename "$up")"
+      fi
+    done <"$STATE"
+    log "pre/$2: removed $n upstream port(s), skipped $skipped; $(state)"
+    # S3 wake off on every PCIe root port (see the header); not restored.
+    w=""
+    for rp in /sys/devices/pci0000:00/0000:*; do
+      [[ $(cat "$rp/class" 2>/dev/null) == 0x0604* ]] || continue
+      echo disabled > "$rp/power/wakeup" 2>/dev/null
+      w="$w$(basename "$rp")=$(cat "$rp/power/wakeup" 2>/dev/null) "
+    done
+    log "pre/$2: S3 wake: $w"
+    # Settle: wait for the (now childless) Thunderbolt root ports to runtime-suspend, cap 5 s.
+    roots=$(roots_from_state)
+    if [[ -n $roots ]]; then
+      t0=$(date +%s%N)
+      for ((i = 0; i < 50; i++)); do
+        ok=1
+        for rp in $roots; do [[ $(cat "$rp/power/runtime_status" 2>/dev/null) == suspended ]] || ok=0; done
+        (( ok )) && break
+        sleep 0.1
+      done
+      ms=$(( ($(date +%s%N) - t0) / 1000000 ))
+      if (( ok )); then log "pre/$2: settled in ${ms} ms"; else log "pre/$2: WARNING settle cap hit after ${ms} ms - continuing"; fi
+    fi
+    ;;
+  post)
+    echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan 2>/dev/null || log "post/$2: WARNING rescan write failed"
+    for ((i = 0; i < 4; i++)); do (( $(xhci) >= 3 )) && break; sleep 0.5; done
+    if (( $(xhci) >= 3 )); then
+      log "post/$2: tree back after attempt 1 (~$((i * 500)) ms): $(state)"
+    else
+      log "post/$2: attempt 1 short after 2 s: $(state) - retrying in a transient unit"
+      systemd-run --quiet --no-block --collect --unit="thunderbolt-remove-rescan-retry-$(date +%s)" \
+        "$0" retry "$2" || log "post/$2: WARNING systemd-run failed; no further attempts"
+    fi
+    ;;
+  retry)
+    for ((a = 2; a <= 6; a++)); do
+      sleep 2
+      echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan 2>/dev/null
+      sleep 0.5
+      if (( $(xhci) >= 3 )); then log "post/$2: tree back after attempt $a: $(state)"; exit 0; fi
+      log "post/$2: attempt $a short: $(state)"
+    done
+    log "post/$2: WARNING tree NOT back after 6 attempts: $(state) - it returns after the next sleep of a few minutes"
+    ;;
+esac
+exit 0

@@ -0,0 +1,25 @@
+# Keep Wi-Fi and USB-C working across suspend on the 2016-2017 Touch Bar
+# MacBook Pros (Apple T1 generation: Alpine Ridge Thunderbolt, BCM43602 Wi-Fi).
+#
+# Two system-sleep hooks, both measured on a MacBookPro14,2:
+# - brcmfmac-reload: the BCM43602 firmware sometimes dies in S3 while its
+#   registers stay readable, and brcmfmac's hot-resume path then leaves Wi-Fi
+#   down until a reload. Unloading before sleep and reloading after makes every
+#   resume take the working path.
+# - thunderbolt-remove-rescan: the firmware powers the Thunderbolt controllers
+#   off in S3, the kernel cannot re-allocate their bridge windows on resume, and
+#   USB-C is dead until a power cycle. Removing the upstream ports before sleep
+#   and rescanning after brings the tree back. See the hooks for the details and
+#   the measured limits.
+product_name="$(cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name 2>/dev/null || true)"
+
+if [[ $product_name =~ MacBookPro13,[123]|MacBookPro14,[123] ]]; then
+  echo "Detected $product_name; installing the suspend hooks for Wi-Fi and USB-C"
+
+  sudo mkdir -p /usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep
+  for hook in brcmfmac-reload thunderbolt-remove-rescan; do
+    sudo install -m 0755 -o root -g root -T \
+      "${OMARCHY_PATH:-/usr/share/omarchy}/default/systemd/system-sleep/$hook" \
+      "/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/$hook"
+  done
+fi

@@ -0,0 +1,20 @@
+echo "Keep Wi-Fi and USB-C working across suspend on 2016-2017 Touch Bar MacBook Pros"
+
+# The install-time fix only reaches machines set up after it shipped. See
+# install/hardware/apple/fix-t1-suspend.sh and the two hooks it installs.
+OMARCHY_PATH="${OMARCHY_PATH:-/usr/share/omarchy}"
+product_name="$(cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name 2>/dev/null || true)"
+[[ $product_name =~ MacBookPro13,[123]|MacBookPro14,[123] ]] || exit 0
+
+for hook in brcmfmac-reload thunderbolt-remove-rescan; do
+  source="$OMARCHY_PATH/default/systemd/system-sleep/$hook"
+  destination="/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/$hook"
+  # A hook the user already carries with the same content is left alone;
+  # anything else is replaced with the packaged copy.
+  if [[ -f $destination ]] && cmp -s "$source" "$destination"; then
+    continue
+  fi
+  sudo mkdir -p /usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep
+  sudo install -m 0755 -o root -g root -T "$source" "$destination"
+done
+# The hooks take effect at the next suspend; nothing to restart.

comments.body:
**MacBookPro14,3 hardware follow-up — 2026-09-19**

Additional observations from the dual-GPU MacBookPro14,3 may help research alongside the MacBookPro14,2 results here. The local trials below used related, guarded experiments, **not this PR's exact hooks**; they do not establish a regression in this PR or successful S3 support on 14,3. Reliable low-power platform suspend remains unresolved. The related T1 driver and earlier hardware results are documented in [my comment on the package PR](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy-pkgs/pull/298#issuecomment-5736510540).

Environment: Omarchy `4.0.4-1`, kernel `7.2.5-3-omarchy`, firmware `529.140.2.0.0`; i7-7820HQ, Intel HD 630 plus Radeon Polaris `1002:67ef` / subsystem `106b:0179`, BCM43602 `14e4:43ba`, Alpine Ridge Thunderbolt. Local T1 package `0.1.r2.ga33c7eb-2`, based on `monomyth/t1-touchbar@a33c7eb`, with `skip_acpi_power=1`. This is one machine. The baseline kernel already has out-of-tree/unsigned modules (taint 12288).

Topology on the tested boot: Radeon `01:00.0`, Samsung NVMe `02:00.0`, Wi-Fi `03:00.0` behind `00:1c.0`; Thunderbolt upstream branches `04:00.0` and `7a:00.0` behind `00:01.1`/`00:01.2`. These are observations, not portable addresses for a script. An older local “NVMe” service incorrectly targeted the Radeon; it was removed, without resolving package idle or S3 recovery.

**New findings that may save other researchers time:**

1. **Readable Wi-Fi PCI registers do not establish recovered firmware.** Preventing D3cold on the BCM43602 and its root port can restore PCI access while `brcmf_msgbuf_query_dcmd` still times out and NetworkManager cannot initialize the interface. PCI inventory and successful pre/post hooks were insufficient success criteria.

2. **Repeated Wi-Fi module teardown has a separate crash path.** The second awake unload with P2P enabled produced an Oops in `_cfg80211_unregister_wdev`, called through `brcmf_p2p_ifp_removed`, during module removal; the fault involved `0xdead000000000122`. This identifies the observed failure path, not its underlying corruption source. Adding P2P disable to the existing feature mask (`0x82000` → `0x82010`) and rebooting removed P2P from supported interface modes. **Two subsequent awake unload/reload cycles passed**, including reconnect and HTTPS 200, with no new Oops/taint. This is a limited mitigation, not proof of reliable recovery from suspended or already-wedged firmware.

3. **A successful PM rehearsal did not predict actual S3 recovery.** A local combination of no-P2P Wi-Fi unload/reprobe, temporary Wi-Fi endpoint/root-port D3cold protection, removal/rescan of empty Thunderbolt branches, and a scoped Radeon reset bypass passed `pm_test=platform`: GPU/device recovery, HTTPS and cleanup succeeded. The otherwise corresponding **real S3 test failed**. Actual low-level firmware resume occurred after approximately **3.32 seconds** of sleep, despite a 45-second RTC target, followed by approximately **19.63 seconds** of awake transitions. Radeon reported:

   ```text
   amdgpu: SMU load firmware failed
   amdgpu 0000:01:00.0: PM: failed to resume async: error -22
   ```

   Thunderbolt did not re-enumerate; fresh BCM43602 firmware initialization was logged, but connection/HTTPS recovery failed amid the GPU/platform failure. The very short S3 interval is a confounder for Thunderbolt recovery. This was not a verbatim test of #11570.

4. **Skipping the pre-S3 Radeon reset was insufficient.** A temporary, model/PCI-ID-restricted kretprobe forced `amdgpu_acpi_should_gpu_reset()` false only for the S3 target. The failing real S3 run recorded `seen=1`, `overridden=1`, `missed=0`; the SMU failure preceded the later recovery reset. The bypass was removed. This rules out that single bypass as a sufficient fix; it does not establish the complete GPU failure mechanism.

5. **Changing CPU profiles works, but did not unlock deeper package idle.** EPP changed from performance to power; measured PC6–PC10 residency remained zero. `MSR 0xE2 = 0x40000008` was read as unlimited/unlocked for this CPU, so no speculative MSR writes were made. Forced ASPM/powersave/powersupersave did not establish deeper package residency and were reverted. PMC LTR reads were all `0xffffffff`; they are not usable evidence for choosing an LTR blocker or an `LTR_IGNORE` write.

6. **Sleep selection and consumption need separate verification.** This installation's `SuspendState=freeze` selects s2idle despite `[deep]` appearing in `/sys/power/mem_sleep`. An actual five-minute s2idle test accumulated no PC6–PC10 time, lost Wi-Fi/Thunderbolt, and the owner observed fans and keyboard lighting throughout. Its approximately 7.23 W battery estimate covers the whole 394.54-second measurement interval, including 92.60 seconds awake/transitions; **it is not a pure-sleep power measurement**. A separate awake CPU/GPU comparison showed roughly 8.24→4.80 W CPU package draw under power-saver and 13.09→8.19 W Radeon draw under forced-low policy. Those policies were restored, and neither result demonstrates suspend power. Purported screen-off samples were rejected because recorded DPMS state remained on.

**Firmware leads, still hypotheses:** locally disassembled ACPI exposes `_S3`; FADT does not advertise low-power S0 idle. `_PTS` has different S3 GPIO/EC preparation under `!OSDW()`. `_WAK` gates the Thunderbolt `PEG1/PEG2.ICMB()` calls and Wi-Fi `RP01/ARPT` wake notifications behind that same non-Darwin branch. These are concrete code paths to investigate, not proof they cause the failures. A global `acpi_osi=!Darwin` experiment was retired after two reported keyboard failures at **login after boot, before session start**; captured fallback boots lacked the override, so causality and execution of the intended test path are unconfirmed. It is not a recommended workaround. The desktop lock screen was unaffected; an unrelated lock-focus experiment was reverted.

**Useful next work:** isolate Radeon SMU/firmware restoration across actual S3; explain the unexpectedly early wake; then validate Wi-Fi reprobe plus PCI protection across real sleep, with empty Thunderbolt branches and repeated successful recovery. Inspect the ACPI branch differences without assuming a global OS override is safe. Intel/GMUX is another unvalidated route: the internal panel currently works through AMD while i915 fails eDP link initialization; do not assume merely detecting the Intel GPU makes it a working alternative.

For comparisons on this model, record actual suspend entry/exit, real firmware resume versus `pm_test`, elapsed sleep versus transition time, fresh network traffic, complete NHI/xHCI rediscovery and functional USB, and measured battery draw. `PM: suspend exit`, a visible Wi-Fi interface, cached PCI D3hot, or a working Touch Bar alone does not establish successful platform recovery. The local guarded experiments refused attached external devices and used explicit preparation/cleanup checks; none of these experimental sleep changes has been enabled as a permanent fix. No firmware, unique machine identifiers or raw desktop logs accompany this update.

**MacBookPro14,1 (2017 13", no Touch Bar, single JHL6540): confirmed, and here it presents as a resume hang, not just dead USB-C**

Independently arrived at the same remove-before-sleep / rescan-after-resume fix on a MacBookPro14,1 before finding this PR. Data in case it helps get it merged — the 14,1 is in your `MacBookPro14,[123]` gate and needs it.

**Symptom on 14,1** (Omarchy 4.0.4, kernel 7.2.5-3-omarchy, `deep`): close lid → `PM: suspend entry (deep)` is the last journal line, black screen on lid open, power-button hold to recover. Every single suspend, not after a loop of cycles. s2idle behaves the same.

**Why it looks like a hard hang.** Bisected with `/sys/power/pm_test` + `pm_print_times=1`. At `pm_test=processors` (no firmware S3 involved at all) the machine *does* come back, but noirq resume takes 77 s:

```
[  656.228] PM: suspend entry (deep)
[  656.891] pcieport 0000:05:00.0: Unable to change power state from D0 to D3hot, device inaccessible   <- TB tree already gone at suspend_noirq
[  656.891] pcieport 0000:05:02.0: Unable to change power state from D0 to D3hot, device inaccessible
[  656.894] pcieport 0000:04:00.0: Unable to change power state from D0 to D3hot, device inaccessible
[  668.140] pcieport 0000:04:00.0: PM: pci_pm_resume_noirq returned 0 after 6038889 usecs
[  668.141] pcieport 0000:05:0[124].0: Unable to change power state from D3cold to D0, device inaccessible
[  669.308] thunderbolt 0000:06:00.0: not ready 1023ms after resume; giving up
[  673.255] tb_cfg_read: -108   (WARNING drivers/thunderbolt/ctl.c:1131, tb_switch_reset <- tb_resume_noirq)  x6
[  673.262] thunderbolt 0000:06:00.0: PM: pci_pm_resume_noirq returned 0 after 3953488 usecs
[  738.555] xhci_hcd 0000:07:00.0: not ready 65535ms after resume; giving up
[  738.556] pcieport 0000:05:02.0: PM: pci_pm_resume_noirq returned 0 after 70416423 usecs
[  739.716] PM: noirq resume of devices complete after 77617.658 msecs
```

A second run stalled 35 s in `04:00.0 pci_pm_resume_noirq`. With a real S3 in between, the screen stays black for well over a minute, and everyone (me included) hard-reboots long before `suspend exit` would have been logged. So on this model the same root cause you describe is a de-facto unusable suspend, which is probably why 14,1 owners report "never resumes" rather than "USB-C dead".

**With the hook** (my minimal version: `echo 1 > 0000:04:00.0/remove` + root-port `power/wakeup=disabled` in `pre`, `echo 1 > 0000:00:1c.4/rescan` in `post`): `pm_test=processors` round trip 7 s, noirq resume 35 ms; `rtcwake -m mem -s 30` and real lid-close suspends resume in ~2 s. The TB tree re-enumerates fine on rescan (xhci comes back on a new bus number, 2d:00.0, as you note). Half a dozen cycles so far, including short sleeps.

**Two other data points:**
- The `brcmfmac-reload` half was not needed on the 14,1 (BCM4350, not BCM43602): with only the Thunderbolt hook installed, Wi-Fi reconnects on its own ~5 s after wake.
- Careful with hook placement when testing: systemd 261 on Omarchy only executes `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/`; `/etc/systemd/system-sleep/` is silently ignored. Lost an afternoon to that. Your installer already uses `/usr/lib`, so that's fine.

Will also report the kernel side (thunderbolt/PCI PM spending 70 s on a controller the platform has powered off) to the upstream thunderbolt maintainers.

**MacBookPro14,1 follow-up: retracting "brcmfmac-reload not needed" — it is, and the failure mode on the BCM4350 is worse than a driver reload can fix**

Correction to my comment above. After a few more hours with only the Thunderbolt hook installed, the 14,1's BCM4350 hit exactly the failure this PR's `brcmfmac-reload` guards against, and it took a full power-off to recover. Both hooks belong in the `MacBookPro14,[123]` gate.

**What happened.** Four deep-sleep cycles resumed cleanly with Wi-Fi reconnecting on its own. The fifth entered S3 and woke back out immediately — `Preparing to enter system sleep state S3` to `Low-level resume complete` is ~3 ms apart in the log, `suspend entry` to `suspend exit` under 4 s. brcmfmac took its hot-resume path on a chip whose firmware had been interrupted mid-D3, and it never answered again:

```
17:28:15.035  PM: suspend entry (deep)
17:28:18.202  ACPI: PM: Preparing to enter system sleep state S3
17:28:18.205  ACPI: PM: Low-level resume complete
17:28:18.925  PM: suspend exit
17:28:21.000  ieee80211 phy4: brcmf_msgbuf_query_dcmd: Timeout on response for query command
17:28:21.000  ieee80211 phy4: brcmf_cfg80211_get_channel: chanspec failed (-5)
   ...every command from here on, forever...
18:12:44.964  ieee80211 phy4: brcmf_run_escan: error (-12)
18:12:44.964  ieee80211 phy4: brcmf_cfg80211_scan: scan error (-12)
```

Scanning and connecting were dead for the rest of the session. Every subsequent suspend then failed as well, because the driver could not put the dead chip into D3 (`brcmf_pcie_pm_enter_D3: Timeout` → `PM: Some devices failed to suspend` → systemd falls back to s2idle → same failure → `Failed to put system to sleep`). So on the 14,1 a wedged Wi-Fi chip also takes suspend down with it.

**Why a driver reload alone would not have recovered it.** On the 14,1 the chip went fully off the PCIe bus, not just "registers readable, firmware dead" as you describe for the 43602 on the 14,2. `modprobe -r brcmfmac; modprobe brcmfmac` and even a warm reboot both failed to probe:

```
brcmfmac: brcmf_chip_recognition: MMIO read failed: 0xffffffff
brcmfmac: brcmf_pcie_probe: failed 14e4:43a3
```

Only a shutdown with the charger unplugged brought it back. So `brcmfmac-reload` is needed here as *prevention* — unload before sleep so the chip gets a clean firmware shutdown and never sits in the half-D3 state that the early wake catches it in — rather than as recovery.

**Suggested addition to the hook: drop the Wi-Fi root port as an S3 wake source.** Out of the box the BCM4350's root port is armed:

```
$ grep RP09 /proc/acpi/wakeup
RP09	  S3	*enabled   pci:0000:00:1d.0
```

Nothing on Omarchy configures Wake-on-WLAN, so this wake source does no useful work, and a PME glitch from a card mid-power-transition is a plausible source of the instant wake that started all this (I could not prove the wake reason from the log, so treat this as a hypothesis). One line in `pre` covers it: `echo disabled > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<wifi root port>/power/wakeup` — the same thing `thunderbolt-remove-rescan` already does for the Alpine Ridge port. The root port can be found generically from the brcmfmac device's parent (`readlink -f /sys/bus/pci/drivers/brcmfmac/0000:*/..`).

**With the reload + wakeup-disable hook in place** (minimal version below, same shape as yours): a 97 s deep sleep, driver deregistered before `suspend entry`, firmware re-downloaded after `suspend exit`, NetworkManager reassociated within a couple of seconds. Will report back if the early wake recurs.

```bash
RP=/sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:1d.0   # RP09, WiFi root port on 14,1
case "$1" in
  pre)  echo disabled > $RP/power/wakeup; modprobe -r brcmfmac_wcc brcmfmac ;;
  post) modprobe brcmfmac ;;
esac
```

Full filtered journal of the failed boot (the successful cycles, the early-wake cycle, the cascade of failed suspends, the failed probe after warm reboot, the clean probe after the cold boot) added to the gist: https://gist.github.com/spamnbeans/819fde7de388f7899d5c11a149685aa6 — `wifi-bcm4350-early-wake-wedge.txt`.
